result.killer: No single product kills it. Against it: a market of about 3,700 registered associations (IPA newsletter figure, unconfirmed), a free IPA registry plus free IPA field help, a one-off rush that ends 30 June 2027, and buyers with little cash.
result.reason: I found no dedicated product that does association re-registration, but the market looks too small to support a business. An IPA 2026 newsletter, as summarised by search, gives about 3,694 associations on the registry (I couldn't open the PDF to confirm the date or scope). NBC reports 162 in Milne Bay, which fits a national total of a few thousand. The buyers are mostly cash-poor churches and clubs. The IPA online registry is free, re-registration costs nothing until 30 June 2027, and IPA teams help executives fill in the forms on the ground. Port Moresby company-secretarial firms already file with the IPA online as authorised persons. After the 2027 rush, ongoing revenue depends on annual returns. I couldn't confirm annual-return fees, audit thresholds or the opt-outs for mutual-benefit associations.

coverage.category: 1. Household employers: domestic workers, live-in carers, nannies
coverage.found: No PNG statute specific to household employment found. Compulsory super applies only to employers of 15 or more (inference: households fall outside). PNGTUC has asked for domestic worker protections and a minimum wage. Nothing new beyond K09.

coverage.category: 2. Scrap-metal dealers
coverage.found: One search returned only other countries' laws (Fiji, Zambia, UK, NZ). No PNG scrap-metal licensing regime found, so unverified whether one exists.

coverage.category: 3. Second-hand dealers and pawnbrokers
coverage.found: Second-hand Dealers Act (Ch. 322) and Pawnbrokers Act (Ch. 93) exist on PacLII. Licensing is by Police, or Public Health for clothing. Licensees must keep a purchase record book and hold goods for 3 days. NCDC trading licence page lists K250 for second-hand dealers. Small, old, paper-based regime.

coverage.category: 4. Gold and jewellery buyers
coverage.found: Domestic gold trade has been open since the 1987 deregulation. Only export is licensed, by BPNG (K25,000 paid-up capital, K75,000 bond, annual licence). That is covered by K04. No separate domestic buyer duty found.

coverage.category: 5. Used car parts and vehicle dismantlers
coverage.found: No dedicated search. Budget used. One RTA hit says its new IT system will cover licensing of motor car dealers and inspection stations; dismantlers were not checked.

coverage.category: 6. Livestock traders, markets and animal transport
coverage.found: Only a colonial-era livestock movement regulation (1951) and NAQIA import permits found. No current domestic movement permit regime confirmed. Nothing actionable.

coverage.category: 7. Small abattoirs and butchers
coverage.found: Slaughtering Act 1964 and Slaughtering Regulation 1965: slaughterhouse licence (K20 a year) and a mandatory daily slaughter record book, with meat inspectors. Current administrator (NAQIA or other) not confirmed. Very small, paper-based market.

coverage.category: 8. Beekeepers
coverage.found: No search spent. Budget. PNG apiculture is minor and no registration duty was seen.

coverage.category: 9. Veterinary practices and veterinary medicine sellers
coverage.found: Veterinary Surgeons Act 1966 sets a Board and Register run by a department Registrar. No veterinary medicines registration or dealer scheme found. Tiny buyer group.

coverage.category: 10. Well drillers and water abstraction
coverage.found: Water use is vested in the State (Environment Act 2000 s79). CEPA issues environment permits for water extraction. The Water Resources Regulation 1982 has unconfirmed status. No borehole driller licence found.

coverage.category: 11. Septic, sanitation and waste haulers
coverage.found: Local governments contract private collectors in towns. CEPA has a permit to discharge waste. No septic-hauler register or recurring report found.

coverage.category: 12. Lift, boiler and pressure-equipment owners and inspectors
coverage.found: Only the Industrial Safety (Lifts) Order 1968 under the Industrial Safety, Health and Welfare Act 1961 was found. Current inspection and certificate practice, and boiler rules, are unverified.

coverage.category: 13. Small water systems
coverage.found: No search spent. Budget.

coverage.category: 14. Pesticide and fertiliser dealers and applicators
coverage.found: Environmental Contaminants (Pesticides) Regulation 1988 under the Environmental Contaminants Act 1978 requires a permit to import, distribute or sell pesticides (K20 application, K100 grant) and records of imports and sales. Administering agency and current enforcement unconfirmed. No fertiliser regime found.

coverage.category: 15. Labour contractors and recruitment agencies
coverage.found: Employment Act (Ch. 373) defines employment agents and worker-recruiters. A PNG firm claims an Employment Agents Licence from the Department of Labour. The Department is the only authorised recruiter for the Australian seasonal worker programme. No recurring-report duty found.

coverage.category: 16. Cemeteries, burial societies and funeral services
coverage.found: Cemeteries Act (Ch. 302): the Minister licenses private burial grounds, e.g. for churches. The Act is under law-reform review. NCDC has acted against a funeral home. No funeral director licence or recurring filing found.

coverage.category: 17. Community and religious bodies: associations, charities, halal and kosher supervision
coverage.found: Strong finding. Associations Incorporation Act 2023 commences 1 July 2026. Every incorporated association, and overseas nonprofits, must re-register online by 30 June 2027, or be removed from the register (restorable for 2 years with a late fee). New duties: public/members-benefit subtype, at least 3 committee members with 1 resident, audited accounts above thresholds, annual returns, beneficial-ownership register. IPA says only 1 of 162 Milne Bay associations had re-registered. Halal and kosher not applicable.

coverage.category: 18. Transport operators: minibus, taxi, moto-taxi, small trucking and bus fleets
coverage.found: The RTA licenses PMVs, taxis and private hire cars (Form 13, renewal needs registration, roadworthiness and fit-and-proper proof). Single-province operations are licensed by the provincial government. A new cloud RTA system is to cover PMV, taxi, freight and dealer licensing. Enforcement drive announced for April 2026. Cash-based sector; see K09.

coverage.category: 19. Market traders, street vendors, money changers
coverage.found: BPNG lists about 9 licensed money changers (Oct 2025), too few to sell to. NCDC trading licences are annual and issued in person, with market stalls charged K5 a day. Informal, per K09.

coverage.category: 20. Small licensed premises with inspections: tattoo studios, driving schools, childminders and nurseries, small food producers, hunting outfitters
coverage.found: No driving-school or instructor licence found on the RTA site. No childcare licensing framework found; early childhood services are still being set up with UNICEF. Small food producers not searched. Tattoo studios and hunting outfitters not applicable.

coverage.category: 5. Used car parts and vehicle dismantlers
coverage.found: No PNG licence or register for dismantlers, wreckers or used-parts dealers found in two searches plus the RTA page. The only vehicle-trade regime is the Motor Car Dealers Act 1976 (amended 2017): anyone selling 3 or more vehicles in 12 months for profit must hold a dealer licence (Form 81, K1,000 licence or renewal fee, K3,000 deposit, 12-month term, per-premises licence, inspectors can inspect the dealer's second-hand vehicle and transaction records). The RTA page (https://www.rta.gov.pg/?p=289) does not mention dismantlers, parts, inspection stations or an online system. Vehicle dealers are a small, licensed group with a records duty, but no filing or reporting duty was seen; nothing new beyond a weak dealer-register idea. coverage.category: 8. Beekeepers
coverage.found: No current hive or apiary registration duty found. Honey is produced mostly in Eastern Highlands, with a few producers in Oksapmin and Bougainville. No export-certification rule for PNG honey was found. Not a mandatory recurring workflow, so nothing to build on.

coverage.category: 13. Small water systems
coverage.found: Water supply is under the National Water Supply and Sanitation Act 2016 (Water PNG Ltd is the sole utility in declared districts, with delegation to local-level governments possible, and ICCC price control on Water PNG). Water abstraction permits fall under the Water Resources Act 1982 (small scheme of 5,000 m3 a year or less costs K10) and the Environment Act 2000 (CEPA permits). Rural systems are run by community WASH committees under the 2015-2030 WASH policy and District WASH Committees (pilot in 12 districts from 2019; ABG WASH Strategy 2024-2029 launched July 2025). No licence or periodic return for private or small operators was found. Donor-run and non-commercial, so there is no software buyer. Unverified: whether the 1982 Water Resources Act is still operative.

coverage.category: 36. Liquor licensing (provincial liquor licensing commissions)
coverage.found: Real, recurring regime. The Liquor (Licensing) Act Ch. 312 (consolidated to 1985 only; full text was not retrievable) sets out licence classes: bottle-shop, dealer's, storekeeper's, canteen, club, publican and others. Licensing is split between provincial commissions and boards and the NCD Liquor Licensing Law 1984, so rules differ by province. NCD: licence year is January to December; annual fees in kina are Publican/Tavern 21,400; Limited Hotel 10,700; Dealer (Bottleshop) 10,700; Restaurant 2,675; Club 321 plus K10 per member; Cabaret 50,000; Special 600; application and issuance fees K100 each. Renewal package: planning and building approvals, Food Safety Management Plan for food-serving venues, proof of land tax and garbage rates paid, club membership list. Filing is in person at the NCDC Licensing Division (Mon-Wed); no online process is confirmed (the site lists 'Liquor License' under Online Services but the content was not shown). NCDC publishes lists of new applications for public objection (one notice listed 23 applications: 9 bottleshop, 5 restaurant, 4 distributor, 4 storekeeper, 1 tavern; its dates are inconsistent). Provincial examples: Morobe board revoked guest-house licences and runs its own renewals (2011); Western Highlands passed a new provincial liquor law in Nov 2018; New Ireland District Court (2010) held selling after expiry is unlicensed (K2,000 fine, stock forfeited). Reform signals: the FTI Consulting report on illicit alcohol launched 1 Jul 2025 (71% of urban alcohol illicit), PM Marape ordered a review of alcohol laws dating from the 1950s, and PNG Customs announced an Excise Act moratorium on new alcohol-manufacturing licences in Oct 2025 (date given as 14 or 19 Oct; the notice page returned 503, so this comes from the search summary only). Unchecked: the Act's current text and amendments, fees outside NCD, the number of licensees nationwide, and whether the NCDC Liquor License online service handles renewals.

result.competitor: The IPA online registry is free, and re-registration is free during the grace period. IPA runs awareness teams that help executives fill in documents (NBC, Alotau). Searches found no dedicated software or service for association re-registration or annual compliance. PwC, PSDI and Hivos have published notes only. Generic Port Moresby law and accounting firms that do IPA filings are a likely substitute (not individually verified).
result.duty: Associations Incorporation Act 2023, in force 1 July 2026 (IPA notice; Hivos alert). All existing associations, including overseas nonprofits, must re-register online by 30 June 2027 or be struck off. Late filers pay penalty fees after the grace period. After that come annual returns, accounting records, audited statements above thresholds (amounts not found) and a beneficial-ownership record in the member register. I did not check the penalty amounts or audit thresholds against the Act text (not reached). Whether filing agents may act for an association is unverified.
result.market: About 3,694 associations, per the IPA Invest PNG newsletter of January 2026 (as reported in search snippets; the PDF text could not be read). NBC reports that IPA's Company Examiner said all associations nationally were removed from the central registry pending re-registration. In Milne Bay, 1 of 162 had re-registered by about August 2026. I found no national re-registration count.
result.reason: The duty is real. IPA material says the Associations Incorporation Act 2023 took effect on 1 July 2026. Every association must re-register online by 30 June 2027 or face strike-off and penalty fees, and must then file an annual return each year, keep records, hold a beneficial-ownership register and, above set thresholds, file audited accounts. I found no dedicated software or done-for-you service. But the IPA portal is free, re-registration costs nothing, and IPA teams help committees in the field. The market is small: an IPA January 2026 newsletter gives about 3,694 associations, mostly cash-poor churches and clubs. The rush is a one-off, with only a light annual return afterwards. Low uptake (1 of 162 in Milne Bay) shows the pain is real, but willingness to pay is weak.

result.competitor: The core job is already covered for free by the state. IPA 2026 newsletters, as quoted in search snippets, say the IPA Online Registry automatically emails agents, business-name owners and company directors when renewals or annual returns are due. One reminder goes 1 month before the annual return due date and another 1 month after it passes. Filing itself is done online through the IPA portal. Done-for-you filing is already sold by PwC PNG company secretarial services (annual filings and return lodgement), KPMG, law firms and local accounting firms. The beneficial-ownership filing variant listed under also_reported was not checked (budget), so it remains unverified.
result.duty: The duty is real and in force. Under the Companies Act 1997 (s.215) and Companies Regulation 2015, every PNG company and registered overseas company must file an annual return once each calendar year. After the due date there is one month to file, then a K1,000 late penalty applies. If the penalty and fees are still unpaid 6 months later, the IPA Automated Compliance Program removes the entity from the register; it has been actively deregistering entities since 10 Jan 2025. Business names lapse when not renewed. An IPA Jan 2026 newsletter, as quoted in search snippets, gives the current fees as K250 per annual return, a K1,000 penalty and a K2,500 reinstatement fee. That replaces the K300 / K3,000 figures in the claim. I could not open the newsletter itself (the PDF fetch returned unreadable binary), so these figures are snippet-based.
result.market: The two sources I found give counts that don't match. An older National article (undated) says 63,433 companies and 149,936 business names were registered. The IPA Jan 2026 newsletter snippet lists 42,376 business names, 3,694 associations and 5,010 foreign enterprises registered in 2025, but the snippet doesn't say whether these are current totals or 2025 figures. In 2019 the IPA flagged about 5,000 long-term non-filers. I found no official count of entities deregistered in 2025.
result.reason: The duty is real, recurring and enforced by automatic deregistration. But the claimed gap, a reminder and deregistration-risk tool, is already filled by the free IPA Online Registry. According to the IPA's 2026 newsletters, as quoted in search snippets, the registry emails directors, owners and agents a month before and a month after annual-return and renewal due dates, and filing is done online in the same portal. Done-for-you lodgement is already sold by PwC PNG, KPMG and local accountants. What remains is a thin reminder layer, which falls under the excluded generic tools, or a corporate-secretarial service in a small market (tens of thousands of entities, many dormant) with low willingness to pay. The annual-return fee is only K250. Reinstatement help could be a niche service, but it is not a software opportunity.

result.competitor: I found no PNG-specific AML compliance product or service for DNFBPs. Global AML vendors such as Zigram, and consultancies such as amluae.com, publish PNG content, but it is aimed at banks or UAE firms, not PNG DNFBPs. The KiVA / PNG Law Society CLE on AML duties for lawyers points to training and advisory demand from local firms. I couldn't confirm whether FASU runs goAML or another free online reporting portal: search found nothing, and the annual report was blocked (403). That remains a risk for the reporting part, but it would not cover CDD, risk assessment or record keeping.
result.duty: Duty is real and in force: the AML/CTF Act 2015 (PNG), with FASU (Bank of PNG) as supervisor. Search excerpts of FASU's supervision and enforcement guidance define DNFBPs as real estate agents, dealers in precious metals or stones, lawyers, notaries and other independent legal professionals acting for clients, TCSPs and motor vehicle dealers. The register also has an accounting-firms category. Duties found: s.57 registration, suspicious matter reports when there is reasonable suspicion, threshold transaction reports (a separate duty), and complying with FASU information requests. Refusing a legal records request is an offence. Not verified: SMR deadline, record-keeping period and penalty amounts (PacLII returned 503 and the FASU PDFs returned 403). Enforcement: Zigram (secondary) says FASU issued show-cause notices to law firms. PNG was grey-listed in February 2026 (vendor sources, not checked against FATF), with weak DNFBP supervision among the findings. Frequency is event-driven, plus ongoing CDD and record keeping. There is no calendar filing.
result.market: 202 DNFBPs on the FASU register as at March 2026 (search snippet of the bankpng register page; the page itself returned 403). Zigram (2025, secondary) reports 199 DNFBPs under supervision: 121 law firms and 37 accounting firms, with the remaining roughly 41 split among real estate agents, precious metal dealers and others. Unregistered firms may add some, but the total addressable market is a few hundred firms at most.
result.reason: The duty is real. The AML/CTF Act 2015 is on PacLII. Search-result excerpts of FASU's guidance define DNFBPs as real estate agents, precious metal and stone dealers, lawyers and notaries, TCSPs and motor vehicle dealers. They also mention s.57 registration, SMRs and offences for not producing records. The register lists accounting firms. Secondary sources say PNG was grey-listed in February 2026 and FASU sent law firms show-cause notices. I found no PNG-specific DNFBP compliance product. The market is very small: about 200 registered DNFBPs, mostly law firms (121) and accountants (37). Reporting is triggered by suspicion rather than a calendar. I couldn't confirm whether FASU uses goAML or a free portal. Low frequency, a tiny market and doubtful willingness to pay make this a weak opportunity.

result.competitor: I found no PNG-specific product and no SIA online portal or public permit database. Generic foreign guard-management software (Guardhouse, SecurityTime from Australia, Belfry, TrackTik, Celayix) handles rostering, time and attendance, and licence-expiry tracking but not SIA submissions.
result.duty: Security (Protection) Industry Act 2004 (PNG), in force since 2006; the SIA Registrar was reappointed for 2024-2027 (Gazette G317, 2025). It requires an operating licence and a permit for each guard, plus permit renewal and registers, and sets training standards. Fees are annual: about K11,000 for a large-firm licence and K22 per guard permit, plus 10% GST. Unlicensed firms are referred to the IRC. Prosecution powers were weak; amendments to strengthen them were pending as of 2021, and I found no evidence they passed. Exact renewal period and filing duties were not verified because the PacLII text returned 403.
result.market: 562 licensed companies with 29,445 guards (December 2022; figure cited by Asia Pacific Report and in the claim). The SIA's 2017 estimate was 219 unlicensed firms with 7,649 guards. More than 30,000 guards were licensed in 2018. Guard numbers are concentrated in large firms, so the in-scope long tail is a few hundred small firms.
result.reason: The duty is real. The Security (Protection) Industry Act 2004 (Security Industries Authority, SIA, operating since 2006) requires security companies to hold an operating licence and a permit for each guard. The Act's contents include sections on permit renewal and on registers. Fees are annual (about K11,000 a year for a large firm's licence, K22 per guard permit). I found no SIA online portal and no PNG-specific vendor. Australian guard-rostering tools (Guardhouse, SecurityTime) cover rostering and licence tracking but not SIA filings. The pain is small: fees are cheap and enforcement is weak (14 staff; many firms unlicensed). The market is about 562 licensed firms, with large firms holding most guards. Willingness to pay from the long tail is doubtful. I could not read the Act's text (403), so renewal and filing details are unconfirmed.

Domestic gold buying has been deregulated since 1987, so no BPNG licence applies to buyers. Only exporters need a BPNG licence (1 year, no fee, K25,000 capital, performance bond). That is a handful of firms, the same exporter-narrow problem as K04. MRA's alluvial mining licences (Mining Act 1992, ss. 48-64) apply to citizen miners, not dealers. I found no dealer licence or recurring dealer register duty, and I did not read the Mining Act text. The citizens-only bill is unconfirmed as law. Buyers are tiny, informal and have low willingness to pay. I found no competing software, but the duty is weak.

The duty is real: the Savings and Loan Societies Act 2015 requires BPNG licensing and supervision, and BPNG says new prudential standards are coming. The IFC project runs to June 2026, and I could not confirm the standards were finalised. The market is tiny: the 2023 BPNG speech counted 17 licensed societies. The largest ones have core banking systems. TISA moved to Oracle FLEXCUBE in 2024 and NCSL chose iGCB in 2024, and both vendors cite compliance and reporting as features. Smaller societies are unverified. I found no reporting forms or frequency, and no penalties beyond licensing powers. With about 17 buyers, vendor-covered top tiers and an uncertain standards timeline, a solo founder would find little to sell.

The duty is not yet law. The bill is a draft: TPA ran a validation period on 6-20 July 2026 before sending it to the National Executive Council. I found no sign it has been tabled or passed. I could not read the PDF text, which is compressed, so I can't confirm requirements, fees, renewal frequency or penalties. The existing TPA Accommodation Accreditation Scheme is voluntary and TPA-run. No provider count was published. Likely buyers are informal, low-margin lodges and guest houses with little software uptake. The reform is speculative, with no deadline and no known test of willingness to pay. A tool would be an application and renewal tracker that might never be required.

result.competitor: Generic EUDR tools (e.g. Forest Trackt, Coolset); SGS log export monitoring in PNG
result.duty: EUDR (Regulation (EU) 2023/1115) as amended: simplified declaration for low-risk small primary operators, applying from about 30 Dec 2026 for timber or 30 Jun 2027 for others
result.market: Not found: no register count of PNG small timber or fish exporters. PNG exports are mostly to China.
result.reason: The EU duty is real but falls on EU operators and importers, not PNG exporters. Search summaries say the Council moved application to 30 Dec 2026 for large and medium operators and for small operators already covered by the EU Timber Regulation. Other small primary operators would start 30 June 2027. I did not confirm the Official Journal text. PNG is classed low risk, so a PNG primary producer would only file a one-time simplified declaration, not recurring work. Forest Trends disputes that classification, and benchmarks are under review. PNG log exports are mostly to China, with SGS monitoring and no FLEGT VPA. I found no count of small operators or fish exporters. Buyers are few and PNG-specific demand is weak. Generic EUDR tools exist. This is the same weakness as K02.

Duty is real: NCDC notice says liquor licences expired 30 Dec 2025. Renewal needs planning and building approvals, a Food Safety Management Plan, and land tax and garbage rates paid. Filing is in person at City Hall. NCDC's guide lists annual fees (K21,400 tavern, K10,700 bottleshop) and a December renewal. A 2010 New Ireland case shows selling after expiry is unlicensed. I found no vendor or consultant doing renewal packs. NCDC's homepage lists an online liquor application, but I couldn't confirm it covers renewals. No licensee count found. The market is small and fragmented across provincial boards, and the duty is annual with paper counters. That fits a permit-runner service better than software, so the score is low.

Licensed second-hand dealers and pawnbrokers are a new group with record-book and licence duties; unverified, not a reason to drop.
Slaughterhouses and butchers have a licence and daily record duty; a new group, in scope.
